source.citation: Meza, L. R.; Zelhofer, A. J.; Clarke, N.; Mateos, A. J.; Kochmann, D. M.; Greer, J. R. Resilient 3D hierarchical architected metamaterials. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 112(37), 11502-11507 (2015).
source.quote: We found the experimentally measured stiffness in the hollow second-order half-cells to scale nearly linearly, with relative density as E = 0.015 Eh ρ 1.04 and strength as σ y = 0.026 σ yh ρ 1.17. [Discussion:] Compression experiments revealed the strength and stiffness of the second-order hierarchical half-cells to scale nearly linearly with relative density, which follows analytical and computational predictions for stretching-dominated

scaling.notes: Table 1 row '20 nm Al2O3 | Es 165 GPa | sigma_ys 5,200 MPa | B(B*) 0.015 (0.036) | beta(beta*) 1.04 (1.00) | C 0.026 | gamma 1.17'. Fit is the average of the fits of the two second-order half-cell geometries. Relative density range of the hollow data 1.04E-4 to 1.82E-3 (SI Table S1); the kg/m3 range is derived with rho_s = 2900 kg/m3 (inferred, see sibling records). Absolute computed stiffness was 68.5% higher than experiment on average for hollow samples. Source also says the stiffness definition is ambiguous (several deformation mechanisms) and the 'metamaterial' stiffness is validated by simulation.

scaling.applies_to: Hierarchical hollow 20 nm Al2O3 second-order half-cell nanolattices, Meza et al. 2015
scaling.prefactor_form: sigma_y = C sigma_ys rho_bar^gamma with C = 0.026, gamma = 1.17, sigma_ys = 5,200 MPa (Table 1)

source.citation: Meza, L. R.; Zelhofer, A. J.; Clarke, N.; Mateos, A. J.; Kochmann, D. M.; Greer, J. R. Resilient 3D hierarchical architected metamaterials. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 112(37), 11502-11507 (2015).
source.quote: σ y = 0.026 σ yh ρ 1.17 [...] Table 1 provides a full list of the constituent material properties used and the observed scaling parameters

scaling.notes: Strength = peak load before failure over footprint area; hierarchical hollow samples fail by beam buckling then shell buckling (SI: S_B 14.8-33.3, beam-buckling regime).

scaling.applies_to: 3D-printed and bulk graphene aerogels (Zhu et al. 2015): printed microlattices 16-53 mg/cm3, bulk aerogels 31-123 mg/cm3
scaling.prefactor_form: E ~ rho^2.5 (not normalised by solid density; no prefactor printed; printed microlattices sit about one order of magnitude above the bulk-aerogel line)

source.citation: Zhu, C.; Han, T. Y.-J.; Duoss, E. B.; Golobic, A. M.; Kuntz, J. D.; Spadaccini, C. M.; Worsley, M. A. Highly compressible 3D periodic graphene aerogel microlattices. Nature Communications 6, 6962 (2015).
source.crossref_title: Highly compressible 3D periodic graphene aerogel microlattices
source.quote: In both cases, Young's modulus was found to scale with density as E∝ρ2.5 [exponent superscript in print], consistent with other studies. The similar values of the exponent (∼2.5) indicate both printed and bulk aerogels show the same bending-dominated behaviour under compression.

scaling.notes: Printed-only range read from Fig. 5d is about 16-53 mg/cm3 (= kg/m3); the paper does not print the fitted range. The 'density' is the overall geometric density, but the paper argues stiffness is controlled by the local filament density.

source.quote: ...all of which are larger than the exponents of 1.61 for modulus and 1.76 for strength of alumina hollow nanolattices (11), as well as the exponents of 1.67 for modulus and 2.00 for strength of glassy carbon nanolattices (18).

scaling.notes: SECONDARY: Bauer et al. paper not accessible (Unpaywall: closed). Fitted density range not stated by Zhang et al.; Zhang quotes ~3.2 GPa modulus and ~280 MPa strength at ~0.35 g/cm3 (350 kg/m3), so the data are far above the 100 kg/m3 window and any extrapolation to <50 kg/m3 is a PROJECTION.

gaps: Zheng et al., Science 344, 1373 (2014) (alumina/Ni-P/polymer octet lattices, 'ultralight, ultrastiff'): full text and SM NOT opened (MIT DSpace blocked curl and WebFetch with HTTP 429 / empty 202; science.org 403). No Zheng value recorded. Lead only, NOT verified from a page I read: a web-search snippet attributes 'densities ... ranged from 0.87 kg/m3 to 468 kg/m3 (0.025% to 20% relative density)' to that paper; Spadaccini's NAS chapter (nationalacademies.org/read/21825/chapter/17, opened via WebFetch summary) says the hollow ALD ceramic lattice had 'a relative density of 0.025 percent' with 'wall thickness less than 50 nm' and that stiffness-density is 'approximately linear' across materials (stretch-dominated octet truss) but gives no E or strength numbers. G also unknown.

Jang et al., Nature Materials 12, 893 (2013) (hollow TiN nanolattices): abstract only (tensile strength 1.75 GPa of the TiN walls); no lattice density, E or compressive strength obtained from it. The TiN lattice numbers recorded come from the companion paper Meza & Greer, J Mater Sci 2014 (relative density 1.36%, E = 61.8 MPa, sigma_y = 0.873 MPa); TiN absolute density not stated there, so density_kg_m3 is null.

Jacobsen et al., Carbon 49, 1025 (2011): primary not opened (paywalled); values recorded only as quoted by Zhang et al. 2019 (0.19 g/cm3, 1.1 GPa, 10.2 MPa) - 190 kg/m3 is above the 100 kg/m3 window and no scaling law found.

Bauer et al., Nature Materials 15, 438 (2016): primary not opened; only the exponents 1.67 (E) and 2.00 (strength), and ~0.35 g/cm3 / 3.2 GPa / ~280 MPa, as quoted by Zhang et al. 2019; density range of the fit unknown; densities far above 100 kg/m3.

Eckel et al., Science 351, 58 (2016) (polymer-derived SiOC lattices): primary paywalled and not opened; web searches returned no density/modulus/strength numbers; Zhang et al. 2019 only plot it (Fig. 3, strength ellipse near 0.1-0.4 g/cm3, figure only, not recorded). Nothing sourced.

Per-sample E, strength and density for Meza et al. Science 2014 and PNAS 2015 are only in plots (Fig. 4A,B and Fig. 5A,B) in the files I could open; the tabulated values (if any) in the journal PDFs or in Meza's thesis (server unreachable) were not seen. All E and strength entries for those papers are by-eye readings (+-25%).
PNAS 2015 does not print the solid-alumina density; 0.30 kg/m3 -> relative density 1.04E-4 mapping and rho_s = 2900 kg/m3 are inferences (rho_s = 2900 kg/m3 is printed in Science 2014).
No shear modulus G found for any ceramic/carbon lattice (none of the papers opened measures it). No G below 10 kg/m3 sourced.

No sourced compressive modulus or strength for any ceramic/carbon lattice between 0.3 and 6 kg/m3 other than the single hierarchical hollow-alumina half-cell family of Meza et al. PNAS 2015 (relative density 1.04E-4 to 1.82E-3); no ceramic/carbon lattice measured below 50 kg/m3 other than alumina hollow nanolattices, the Zhu graphene aerogel microlattice (16 kg/m3) and the Chen glassy-carbon microlattices (30-50 kg/m3, density from a secondary source).

Meza et al., Acta Mater. 140, 424 (2017), 'Reexamining the mechanical property space of three-dimensional lattice architectures' (more hollow alumina lattice geometries and a finer scaling analysis): only its SI .docx was opened (CaltechAUTHORS 8zt06-95b70); the main paper was not. Its SI states: 'the experimental results do not follow a true power law scaling, but they appear to follow one in the range of relative densities investigated experimentally' (used as a caveat in the Meza 2014 scaling note).
Surjadi et al., Matter 5, 4029 (2022) hybrid carbon microlattices: not opened (paywalled); densities unknown.
